title: HTML Headings
summary: Headings name the parts of a page. The main title uses h1, and smaller sections can use h2 or h3.
introduction: Headings name the parts of a page. The main title uses h1, and smaller sections can use h2 or h3. Think of a school book with a title, chapters and smaller topics. Give your page the same clear order.
learningObjectives: Use h1 to h6 to express the structure of a page
Keep a logical heading hierarchy without skipping levels
Avoid choosing headings for their visual size

blocks.text: Browsers render `<h1>` largest and `<h6>` smallest by default, but the size is only a default style. The **meaning** is the level of importance: `<h1>` is the title of the whole page, `<h2>` starts a major section, `<h3>` a sub-section within it, and so on.
Think of headings as the table of contents of a document. Each heading introduces the content that follows it until the next heading of the same or a higher level.

blocks.text: Rules that keep the outline meaningful

items: Use **one `<h1>`** per page, describing what the page is about. Multiple `<h1>` elements are technically allowed but make the outline ambiguous.
**Do not skip levels** on the way down: an `<h2>` should be followed by `<h3>`, not `<h4>`. Going back up (from `<h4>` to `<h2>`) to start a new section is fine.
Never pick a heading level **because of its size**. If an `<h2>` looks too big, change it with CSS; do not use an `<h4>` in its place.

Do not use headings for text that is not a heading, such as a bold label or a slogan. Use `

` with `` instead.

blocks.text: The most common mistake is `<h1>` for the site name on every page and another `<h1>` for the article title. Make the site name a link in the header instead and keep the single `<h1>` for the page's main subject.

Screen readers let users list all headings and jump directly to the section they want, which is only useful when the levels are honest. Search engines weigh heading text heavily when deciding what a page is about. The [SEO lesson](/tutorials/html/seo) returns to this point.

The `<hr>` element marks a change of topic inside a section, for example between scenes in a story. It is rendered as a horizontal line, but its meaning is "the subject changes here", not "draw a line".

questions.question: It is fine to use an h4 directly after an h2 if the h3 size looks too large.
questions.explanation: Heading levels describe structure, not size. Skipping from h2 to h4 breaks the outline; change the size with CSS instead.
